title: SPARC Building Scan
text:
Welcome to the SPARC Building Scan page. This website provides an introduction to the Building Scan data product, serves as a guide for technical users, and documents the detailed methodology behind the analysis.
Tier 2 of the SPARC program focuses on tailored analytical products for individual cities. The Building Scan product is designed to provide detailed insights into the building stock of a city, including information on building types, heights, footprints, and other relevant attributes. This enables city planners, policymakers, and investors to make informed decisions regarding urban development, infrastructure planning, and risk assessment.


The Building Scan product generates high-quality, analysis-ready building footprints for a given city. Building footprints are digitized polygons outlining each building across an area of interest. They are a foundational data layer for urban planning, climate risk and resilience analytics, assessments of infrastructure and service gaps, and cadastral systems.
Project teams often default to public sources such as OpenStreetMap or Google Open Buildings. While these are valuable resources, their accuracy varies greatly by location. Their buildings may be outdated or missing in informal and recently developed areas, contain faulty polygons, or lack key attributes. Building Scan provides a consolidated workflow to help teams obtain the most suitable building layer through one of three options.




1. Open-Source Layers


Integrates public datasets (Overture, OSM, 3D GlobFP), with cleaning to remove duplicates and false positives.


Typical use: Investment scoping.






2. AI Extraction


Option 1, supplemented with AI extraction in poorly mapped areas (missing or outdated buildings), using high-resolution satellite imagery and the open-source Segment Anything Model (SAM3).


Typical use: Analytics informing infrastructure operations.






3. Manual Digitization


Digitization carried out by a specialist firm using procured imagery.


Typical use: Taxation, or a complete building registry or cadastral system.

Each building is attributed with the following variables.

Building Heights: Information on the vertical dimension of buildings, which is crucial for urban planning and risk assessment.
Building Age: Information on the age of buildings, which can be important for understanding the historical development of the city and for assessing the need for maintenance or retrofitting.




Cities in developing countries often lack current, reliable, and accessible geospatial data. Existing information is frequently fragmented across analogue or disconnected systems, costly to acquire and analyze, and difficult to reuse because of inconsistent licensing and limited technical capacity. The Smart Parcel Atlas for Resilient Cities (SPARC) program addresses this gap by creating a shared, scalable platform for urban geospatial intelligence. There are three tiers of the SPARC program: 1. Tier 1 — Global urban data and analytics 2. Tier 2 — City-specific geospatial intelligence 3. Tier 3 — Operational uptake and client integration


Provides standardized, quality-assured geospatial data and automated statistics for approximately 10,000 cities worldwide. Supports early operational scoping and serves as a “conversation starter” for country and city engagements. Made available through the SPARC Toolkit on GeoInsights for internal and external users.



Delivers higher-resolution, on-demand analytics for up to 100 priority cities. Supports investment option assessment and site prioritization through six initial services: buildings and parcels; urban public infrastructure; extreme heat exposure; multi-hazard exposure; green infrastructure; and urban settlement forecasts.



Connects SPARC analytics directly to World Bank Group operations and client decision-making. Regional operational teams lead demand identification, client engagement, local validation, and incorporation of findings into projects and local systems.

title: What is SPARC
text:
Cities in developing countries often lack current, reliable, and accessible geospatial data. Existing information is frequently fragmented across analogue or disconnected systems, costly to acquire and analyze, and difficult to reuse because of inconsistent licensing and limited technical capacity. As a result, World Bank Group teams, governments, and private investors may rely on outdated or low-resolution evidence when deciding where to invest in infrastructure, services, resilience, and urban development—slowing project preparation, duplicating costs, and increasing the risk of poorly targeted investments.
The Smart Parcel Atlas for Resilient Cities (SPARC) program addresses this gap by creating a shared, scalable platform for urban geospatial intelligence. The SPARC Toolkit on GeoInsight will combine quality-assured satellite imagery, global and city-specific datasets, standardized analytics, AI-enabled tools, and practical guidance in an interface accessible to non-specialists. There are three tiers of the SPARC program: 1. Tier 1 — Global urban data and analytics 2. Tier 2 — City-specific geospatial intelligence 3. Tier 3 — Operational uptake and client integration


Provides standardized, quality-assured geospatial data and automated statistics for approximately 10,000 cities worldwide. Includes city extent, built-up area, buildings, population, roads, administrative boundaries, and hazard data. Supports early operational scoping and serves as a “conversation starter” for country and city engagements. Made available through the SPARC Toolkit on GeoInsights for internal and external users.



Delivers higher-resolution, on-demand analytics for up to 100 priority cities. Supports investment option assessment and site prioritization through six initial services: buildings and parcels; urban public infrastructure; extreme heat exposure; multi-hazard exposure; green infrastructure; and urban settlement forecasts. Produces data layers, maps, analytical findings, and investment recommendations tailored to operational needs. Uses standardized workflows, centralized procurement, and partnerships to reduce the cost of each city analysis.



Connects SPARC analytics directly to World Bank Group operations and client decision-making. Regional operational teams lead demand identification, client engagement, local validation, and incorporation of findings into projects and local systems. Training, technical guidance, communications materials, and user-friendly GeoInsights tools help non-geospatial specialists interpret and apply the data. Ensures that the global and city-level analytics translate into better-targeted public and private investments.
The program will provide consistent urban data for roughly 10,000 cities worldwide while delivering higher-resolution, on-demand analytics for up to 100 cities in areas such as buildings and parcels, infrastructure access, heat and hazard exposure, green infrastructure, and future urban growth.
By centralizing data procurement, analytical workflows, technical support, and access, SPARC will reduce duplication and costs while improving data reuse across the World Bank Group and its clients. This shared “global technical backbone,” paired with regionally led client engagement, is intended to accelerate project preparation, improve the targeting of public and private investment, and support more resilient, productive, and inclusive urban development.

title: SPARC Building Scan
text:
The SPARC building scan is designed to extract and attribute building footprints for an entire city following a multistep process. To begin, we extract building footprints in the follow order:

Download buildings from Overture maps

Evaluate completeness of the downloaded building footprints through comparison to other built area data:

World Settlement Footprint

GHSL

[POTENTIALLY] Alpha Earth embeddings

Identify areas for infill from #2; perform infill using additional data sources:

HOT OSM tasking

Purchase satellite imagery and run building extraction locally

Purchase extracted building footprints from commercial providers


This notebook will focus on #1 and #2, with #3 being addressed in subsequent steps depending on the solution.

Methodology
text: This page documents the workflow for option 1.

title: Methodology
text:
Data Sources
The Building Scan workflow leverages various open-source geospatial layers to generate building footprints. These layers include:

Overture Maps Buildings
Overture Maps Buildings is a global vector building layer published by the Overture Maps Foundation. Overture conflates several major open and openly licensed footprint sources — OpenStreetMap (OSM), Google Open Buildings, Microsoft Global ML Building Footprints, Esri, and Meta — into a single layer of roughly 2.3 billion footprints, prioritizing community-contributed OSM geometry over machine-learning-derived sources during conflation.
Overture Maps Foundation. (2024). https://docs.overturemaps.org/


3D-GloBFP
3D-GloBFP is the first global building-footprint dataset to include a modeled height for every individual building. Its footprint geometries are drawn primarily from Microsoft’s Global ML Building Footprints (~1.3 billion structures, ca. 2020) and augmented in East Asia with ~280 million building footprints of Shi et al. (2024), produced with their Comprehensive Large-Scale Mapping (CLSM) framework, to address known coverage gaps in the region.
Che, Y., Li, X., Liu, X., Wang, Y., Liao, W., Zheng, X., et al. (2024). 3D-GloBFP: The first global three-dimensional building footprint dataset. Earth System Science Data, 16, 5357–5374. https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-16-5357-2024
The full workflow can be summarized as four distinct steps: data integration, data cleaning, flagging urban areas for review, and height attribution.

title: Methodology
text:
Data Integration
The integration step combines Overture Maps Buildings and 3D-GloBFP building footprint datasets to create a comprehensive and accurate representation a city’s built environment.

Download Overture and 3D-GloBFP for the city’s AOI.
Augment with 3D-GloBFP where it contributes non-duplicate buildings, keeping the most recent footprint (typically Overture).
Assign temporary height values, geometry confidence, and review flag.
